explanations.answer: It's lit up by his glory
explanations.explanation: The text says it plainly: “…the earth was illuminated by his glory.” This angel comes down from heaven with great authority. I flip on the kitchen light before sunrise and feel pretty important. This angel makes my light switch look like a birthday candle.

Shaking isn't what the text gives here. It says the earth “…was illuminated by his glory.” I'm the one who shakes things up, usually when I dive into the chocolate chips. This angel brings light instead.
It's the other way around, friend. The earth “…was illuminated by his glory.” When this angel arrives with great authority, the earth gets lit up. Nobody's fumbling for a flashlight.

That's the news, and he says it twice: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” The angel cries it out in a mighty voice. Then he says what she has become: a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit. I'd say that's a message with some volume behind it.
Not this time. The angel cries out, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” She isn't climbing anywhere. The news goes the opposite direction.

The angel says nothing about her repenting. What he cries out is “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” Then he says what she has become: a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit. The news is about her fall.

Right on the money. The angel says, “She has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast.” That's a big change for the great city. The angel isn't describing a place anybody would want to move into.

This one is true, friend. The angel says, “She has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast.” He says it right after he announces she has fallen. That's what the great city has become.
That's the word. The merchants of the earth “…have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury.” Her luxury was good business for them. I'd say that's a lot of money riding on one city.
The angel says the opposite. The merchants “…have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury.” Her luxury was making them richer, not poorer. Poor isn't in the verse.
The text doesn't use that word. It says the merchants “…have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury.” The angel is talking about money, and how they got it. Humble isn't in the verse.
That's the call: “Come out of her, My people…” It's a voice from heaven, and it speaks to God's own people. The voice doesn't tell them to wait around and see how it goes. It tells them to leave.
The voice says the opposite. It says, “Come out of her, My people…” Staying put isn't the instruction. Leaving is.
No walls come up in this message. The voice says, “Come out of her, My people…” That's a call to leave, not to build. I've been known to patch a cracked cookie, but this isn't that kind of job.
That's it. The voice says to come out “…so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.” Coming out is how they avoid both. That's the warning, plain and simple.

Treasures aren't what the voice has in mind. It says to come out “…so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.” The warning is about sins and plagues. Nobody's being sent out to grab loot.
Songs aren't the word here. The voice says to come out “…so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.” It's a warning about what comes with staying. The word is plagues.
That's what the voice says: “…God has remembered her iniquities.” Her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has not let them slip by. The voice names it flat out. Iniquities means wrongdoing.
The voice doesn't say that. It says her sins are piled up to heaven, and “…God has remembered her iniquities.” Nothing is covered over here. Remembered is the word.
That's not what the voice says. The line is “…God has remembered her iniquities.” Her sins are piled up to heaven, not carried off anywhere. The sins stay on the record.

The voice says, “pay her back double for what she has done…” It goes on to say, “mix her a double portion in her own cup.” Double is the number, and it shows up twice in the same verse. I'd call that a voice making sure you heard it.
Half isn't a number in this verse. The voice says, “pay her back double for what she has done…” It's more, not less. Double is what it asks for.
Ten times is a lot, but it's not the number in the text. The voice says, “pay her back double for what she has done…” It also says to “mix her a double portion in her own cup.” Double is the amount.

explanations.answer: I sit as queen and will never see grief
explanations.explanation: That's what she says in her heart. She says she sits as queen, that she is not a widow, and that she will never see grief. That's a lot of confidence for a city whose sins are piled up to heaven. I think she sounds awfully sure of herself.

explanations.answer: I fear my last day is coming very soon
explanations.explanation: She says nothing like that. In her heart she says, “I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.” Fear isn't in her words. She's talking about never seeing grief.

explanations.answer: I regret the things I have done to others
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show her sorry for anything. In her heart she says she sits as queen and will never see grief. That's the voice of someone who thinks she's safe. Regret isn't in her words.

That's it: “Therefore her plagues will come in one day—death and grief and famine…” She said she'd never see grief, and grief shows up in a single day. After all that bragging, the turnaround is quick. The voice also says she will be consumed by fire.
Seven years doesn't appear in this verse. The voice says her plagues “…will come in one day…” It's quick. One day is the answer.
The voice doesn't describe a slow stretch of time. It says, “…her plagues will come in one day…” That's the opposite of many generations. One day is the answer.

Not quite, friend. The voice says, “…mighty is the Lord God who judges her.” The kings of the earth are the ones who were immoral with her, so they're on the other side of the story. God is the one who judges.
That's right. The voice says, “…mighty is the Lord God who judges her.” The kings aren't the judges here. They were immoral with her, and later they weep over her.

That's what the text says: the kings “…will weep and wail at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her.” They lived in luxury with her. Now they watch the smoke and weep. I think this one is heavy.

The kings aren't cheering. They “…will weep and wail at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her.” Later in the passage, heaven and the saints and apostles and prophets are told to rejoice. These kings weep.

explanations.answer: They will rush in to save her
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show the kings rushing in. They “…will weep and wail…” at the sight of the smoke. Then they stand at a distance and cry out, “Woe, woe to the great city…” Rushing in isn't part of the picture.
That's it. The kings “…will stand at a distance…” in fear of her torment. They watch from far off. Then they cry out, “Woe, woe to the great city, the mighty city of Babylon!”
The text puts them farther away than that. The kings “…will stand at a distance…” They're afraid of her torment, so the gates are out. I think they're keeping their feet where it's safe.
Not inside, friend. The kings “…will stand at a distance…” They're afraid of her torment. Walking in isn't part of the picture.
The kings say the opposite. They cry out, “For in a single hour your judgment has come.” That's not many long years. It's one hour.
Right. The kings cry out, “Woe, woe to the great city, the mighty city of Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.” One hour is the word. No long years anywhere.

explanations.answer: No one is left to buy their cargo
explanations.explanation: That's the reason in the text: “…because there is no one left to buy their cargo…” The merchants weep and mourn over her. Gold, silver, pearls, fine linen and more are on their list. Without a buyer, none of it moves.

explanations.answer: Their ships have all been sunk
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The merchants weep and mourn “…because there is no one left to buy their cargo…” Their problem is no customer. Nobody mentions their ships at this point.

explanations.answer: The kings refused to pay them
explanations.explanation: The kings aren't mentioned in that reason. The merchants weep and mourn “…because there is no one left to buy their cargo…” The text says nothing about a bill. Their reason is no buyer.

That's the opposite of the text. The merchants say, “all your luxury and splendor have vanished, never to be seen again.” Never to be seen again means it's gone for good. There's no someday in that line.
Right. The merchants say, “all your luxury and splendor have vanished, never to be seen again.” Vanished means gone. And never again means no someday.

explanations.answer: Fine linen and purple and scarlet
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. The merchants cry, “Woe, woe to the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls!” It's a picture of her at her fanciest. That's the picture they paint in their cry.

That's not how they remember her. The merchants say she was “…clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls!” They're picturing her richest look. Mourning clothes aren't in the line.

No armor in their picture. The merchants say she was “…clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls!” It's all fine cloth and jewels. Nothing in it is meant for a battle.

explanations.answer: What city was ever like this great city?
explanations.explanation: That's their cry. At the sight of the smoke, they exclaim, “What city was ever like this great city?” They're looking back at how great she was. I think they're still in shock.

explanations.answer: Who will ever rebuild this great city?
explanations.explanation: That's not what they cry out. At the sight of the smoke, they ask, “What city was ever like this great city?” They're looking back at how great she was. Rebuilding doesn't come up.

explanations.answer: Why did no one warn this great city?
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show them asking that. They cry out, “What city was ever like this great city?” Their words are about how great she was. Nobody mentions a warning.

That's the word. They cry, “…where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth!” Everyone who had ships on the sea was enriched by her wealth. Then they cry that in a single hour she has been destroyed.
It's the opposite. They cry, “…where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth!” Her wealth made them richer. The ruin comes with her fall.
Frightened isn't the word in this line. They cry, “…where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth!” Enriched means they got richer from her wealth. That's the word the text uses.

That's right. The merchants “…will stand at a distance, in fear of her torment.” (verse 15). The shipmasters, passengers and sailors “…will stand at a distance…” too (verse 17). The kings do the same (verse 10).

It's true, friend. The merchants “…will stand at a distance, in fear of her torment.” (verse 15). The shipmasters, passengers and sailors “…will stand at a distance…” too (verse 17). They keep their distance, just like the kings.

That's the call: “Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets…” The kings, merchants and sailors mourn her. Heaven and the saints and apostles and prophets get a different message. They're told to rejoice.

That's what the kings, merchants and sailors do. Heaven is told, “Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets…” The two groups aren't on the same page. Heaven gets a call to rejoice.
Praying isn't what the call says. It says, “Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets…” That's a call to rejoice. The text gives no prayer here.
That's the word: “…because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.” God is the one who pronounces it. The saints and apostles and prophets are told to rejoice because of it.

Mercy isn't the word in this verse. It says, “…because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.” That's the reason heaven and the saints and apostles and prophets are told to rejoice. The word is judgment.
Promise isn't what the verse says. It reads, “…because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.” God has spoken His judgment against Babylon. That's the reason to rejoice.

That's what he does. The mighty angel “…picked up a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea…” Then he says what it stands for: “With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again.” He throws it, and then he explains it.

explanations.answer: Sets it at the city gate
explanations.explanation: He doesn't set it down anywhere near a gate. The mighty angel “…cast it into the sea…” That's a throw, not a delivery. The stone ends up in the water.

No breaking in the text. The mighty angel picked up the stone and “…cast it into the sea…” He throws it, and then he says what it stands for. I couldn't even lift a stone that size, so I'm glad this wasn't my job.

That's what he says: “With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again.” The stone he threw into the sea goes along with the words. Never to be seen again is the line to hold on to.
It's true, friend. The mighty angel says, “With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again.” He says it right after he casts the stone into the sea.
The angel says the opposite. “Nor will any craftsmen of any trade be found in you again…” No craftsmen of any trade will be found in her. That covers any trade at all.
Right. The angel says, “Nor will any craftsmen of any trade be found in you again…” That covers any trade at all. The workshops are empty.

explanations.answer: The voices of a bride and bridegroom
explanations.explanation: That's it. The angel says, “…the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again.” It's a happy sound, and it goes quiet in her for good. I think that's one of the saddest lines on the list.

explanations.answer: The cheers of a festival crowd
explanations.explanation: Not a festival crowd. The angel says, “…the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again.” That's a smaller, sweeter sound. It's the voices of a bride and bridegroom.

explanations.answer: The shouts of a winning army
explanations.explanation: No army in this line. The angel says, “…the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again.” It's a happy sound. The voices of a bride and bridegroom.
That's the word: “…because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” The nations were deceived by her sorcery. That's what the angel says.
Healed isn't what the verse says. It reads, “…because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” The nations were deceived by her sorcery. Deceived is the word.
Blessed isn't the word in this verse. The angel says, “…because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” The nations were deceived by her sorcery. Deceived is the word the text uses.

explanations.answer: The blood of prophets and saints
explanations.explanation: That's it: “And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.” I think this is a heavy one, friend. It tells us what was found in her at the very end. It's not a line to hurry past.

No hidden gold gets found. The text says, “And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.” I think this one is heavy. What's found in her is the blood of prophets and saints.

explanations.answer: A scroll of her secret plans
explanations.explanation: No scroll turns up here. The text says, “And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.” I think this is a heavy line. What was found in her was blood.
